items.prompt: What does "declarative configuration" mean in the context of Infrastructure as Code?
choices: Describing the desired end state, not the steps to get there — the tool figures out what needs to change
Writing a script that runs cloud CLI commands in order
Manually clicking through a console to configure resources
A configuration format that only supports one resource at a time
items.explanation: Declarative configuration describes what should exist (e.g. "this server should be size large"), and the tool computes what actually needs to change — as opposed to an imperative script that specifies the exact steps to run.
items.reference:
📝 Declarative — "this should exist, this size"
🤖 Tool's job — figure out what needs to change to get there

Why: describing the end state (not the steps) is what lets a tool safely re-run the same configuration without duplicating work.

items.prompt: How does a declarative IaC file ("web-1: size = large") differ from an imperative script ("resize-server web-1 large")?
choices: The declarative file describes what should exist; the imperative script describes the exact command to run
They are functionally identical in every way
The imperative script is always safer to re-run
Declarative files can only be used for databases, not servers
items.explanation: A declarative file states the desired state and lets a tool compute the difference; an imperative script just specifies commands, with no built-in awareness of current state.
items.reference:
📝 Declarative — "this should exist, this size"
🤖 Tool's job — figure out what needs to change to get there

Why: describing the end state (not the steps) is what lets a tool safely re-run the same configuration without duplicating work.

items.prompt: What is a "state file" in Infrastructure as Code?
choices: The IaC tool's own record of what it last applied, used to compute what's different next time
A file listing every employee who has console access
A backup of the entire cloud provider's infrastructure
A log of every error the tool has ever encountered
items.explanation: The state file is the tool's memory of what it last successfully applied — without it, there's nothing to compare a new plan against, and nothing to detect drift against either.
items.reference:
🧠 State file — the tool's memory of what it last applied
🔍 Used for — computing the next plan, detecting drift

Why: without a state file, a tool has no record of prior reality to compare against — this is exactly what an imperative script lacks.

items.prompt: Why can't an imperative script of cloud CLI commands detect infrastructure drift the way a declarative tool with a state file can?
choices: Because the script has no memory of what it applied before, so it has nothing to compare current reality against
Because imperative scripts are always written in a different programming language
Because drift only happens in declarative systems, never in imperative ones
Because cloud providers block imperative scripts from running twice
items.explanation: Detecting drift requires comparing a remembered prior state against current reality — an imperative script has no such memory, so it has nothing to compare against.
items.reference:
🧠 State file — the tool's memory of what it last applied
🔍 Used for — computing the next plan, detecting drift

Why: without a state file, a tool has no record of prior reality to compare against — this is exactly what an imperative script lacks.

items.prompt: What is a "plan" in the Infrastructure as Code workflow?
choices: A computed list of the specific create/update/delete actions needed, shown before anything is changed
A document written by hand describing future infrastructure goals
The final step that actually changes real infrastructure
A list of every resource that has ever existed
items.explanation: A plan is the computed diff between desired and current state — exactly what would be created, updated, or deleted — shown for review before anything is actually applied.
items.reference:
📋 Plan — computed diff, shown before any change
▶️ Apply — actually executes the plan

Why: separating "compute what would change" from "actually change it" is what lets a human catch a mistake before it happens.

items.prompt: What is "apply" in the Infrastructure as Code workflow?
choices: Actually executing a plan, making the real infrastructure match the declared state
Writing the initial declarative configuration file
Reviewing a plan without making any changes
Deleting the state file
items.explanation: Apply is the step that actually executes the plan's create/update/delete actions against real infrastructure, making it match the declared configuration.
items.reference:
📋 Plan — computed diff, shown before any change
▶️ Apply — actually executes the plan

Why: separating "compute what would change" from "actually change it" is what lets a human catch a mistake before it happens.

items.prompt: What is "drift" in Infrastructure as Code?
choices: Infrastructure that no longer matches its state file, usually from a change made outside the declared configuration
The natural degradation of hardware over time
A planned, deliberate migration between cloud providers
The time delay between writing config and it taking effect
items.explanation: Drift is exactly what the opening scenario describes: a resource was changed directly (through a console, say), so the actual infrastructure no longer matches what the state file records.
items.reference:
📄 State file says — web-1 = small
☁️ Actual cloud — web-1 = xlarge (changed via console)
⚠️ Drift — the two no longer match

Why: this is the exact mechanism behind the opening scenario's outage — a console change nobody recorded.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what specifically caused drift between the state file and the real infrastructure?
choices: The on-call engineer resized web-1 directly in the console during the incident, without updating the declared config
A cloud provider outage corrupted the state file
The IaC tool was uninstalled and reinstalled
The teammate's deploy intentionally introduced drift
items.explanation: The console resize during the incident changed the actual infrastructure but not the state file or declared config — that gap is drift, and it's what caused the teammate's later deploy to silently undo the fix.
items.reference:
📄 State file says — web-1 = small
☁️ Actual cloud — web-1 = xlarge (changed via console)
⚠️ Drift — the two no longer match

Why: this is the exact mechanism behind the opening scenario's outage — a console change nobody recorded.

items.prompt: What does "idempotency" mean for an IaC apply operation?
choices: Applying the same declared configuration twice produces the same result — the second apply is a no-op if nothing changed
Every apply must take exactly the same amount of time
Only one person can run apply at a time
The tool refuses to run apply more than once ever
items.explanation: Idempotency means the end state is the same whether you apply once or apply the same unchanged config again — the second run correctly computes nothing left to do.
items.reference:
1️⃣ First apply — creates real resources
2️⃣ Second apply, same config — computes zero changes

Why: this is what makes it safe to re-run a tool after a failure, without worrying about duplicating anything.

items.prompt: Why does idempotency matter specifically when an apply fails halfway through and gets re-run?
choices: Because the re-run needs to safely create only what's still missing and update only what still differs, without duplicating anything already done
Because a failed apply always corrupts the state file permanently
Because idempotency only matters for the very first apply, never for re-runs
Because re-running after a failure is always forbidden by IaC tools
items.explanation: A safe re-run needs to compute the same plan a fresh run would — only the actually-missing or actually-different parts — which is exactly what a diff-based plan naturally provides.
items.reference:
1️⃣ First apply — creates real resources
2️⃣ Second apply, same config — computes zero changes

Why: this is what makes it safe to re-run a tool after a failure, without worrying about duplicating anything.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why did the teammate's routine deploy accidentally undo the incident fix?
choices: Because the teammate's deploy correctly followed the documented process, which had no record of the console change made during the incident
Because the teammate deliberately reverted the on-call engineer's change
Because the deploy tool had a bug that randomly resized servers
Because the on-call engineer's change was technically invalid
items.explanation: The teammate did nothing wrong by their own process — the console change was never recorded anywhere the deploy process could see, so "undoing" it wasn't a mistake from their perspective at all.
items.reference:
🔥 Incident — console resize, undocumented
💥 Next deploy — resized back, following the documented process exactly

Why: nobody violated their own process — the missing piece is a single source of truth both changes should have gone through.

items.prompt: What would have prevented the outage in the opening scenario, per this unit's framing?
choices: Making the incident-time resize part of the declared configuration, so it became the one source of truth instead of an invisible console change
Firing the on-call engineer for making a manual change
Never allowing any server to be resized under any circumstances
Requiring two engineers to approve every console click
items.explanation: The fix isn't avoiding manual changes entirely — it's making sure a real, necessary change gets reflected in the declared configuration afterward, so it becomes visible and durable instead of invisible drift.
items.reference:
🔥 Incident — console resize, undocumented
💥 Next deploy — resized back, following the documented process exactly

Why: nobody violated their own process — the missing piece is a single source of truth both changes should have gone through.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, what happens when an imperative script is run a second time?
choices: It may run the same command again — safety on a second run depends on the script being written carefully
It automatically detects nothing has changed and skips execution
It always fails with an error the second time
It's functionally identical to a declarative tool's second run
items.explanation: An imperative script has no built-in mechanism to check whether its target command is already true — safety on a repeat run depends entirely on how carefully the script itself was written, unlike a declarative tool's automatic diff.
items.reference:

Running twiceDepends on script careSecond run: no-op

Why: this table row is the concrete reason declarative tools dominate IaC — safety on re-run isn't something you have to get right by hand each time.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, why can't an imperative script detect drift?
choices: Because it doesn't know or check current state — it just runs commands regardless of what's already true
Because imperative scripts are always executed on a schedule
Because drift detection requires a graphical console, not a script
Because scripts can only run on Mondays
items.explanation: An imperative script just executes commands without checking or comparing against current state — there's no diff step where drift could even be noticed.
items.reference:

items.prompt: Why does L2 argue a plan should be reviewed by a human before being applied, rather than applied automatically?
choices: Because the plan's entire value is catching an unexpected delete or unintended change before it happens, not after
Because IaC tools require manual approval by law
Because plans are always wrong and need correction
Because reviewing plans is faster than applying them
items.explanation: The plan step exists specifically so a human can catch something like an accidental delete (from removing the wrong line in a config file) before it actually happens to real infrastructure.
items.reference:
📋 Plan shows — "3 to create, 1 to update, 0 to delete"
👀 Human reviews — catches a mistake before it's real

Why: a plan's value is entirely in being reviewable before commitment — applying blind defeats the point of computing it at all.

items.prompt: What kind of mistake is a plan review specifically well-suited to catch, per L2?
choices: An accidental delete caused by removing the wrong line in a config file, visible in the plan before it's applied
A typo in a code comment that has no effect on infrastructure
A slow network connection to the cloud provider
A missing README file in the repository
items.explanation: A plan surfaces exactly what would be deleted — if that includes something unintended (like a database accidentally removed from the config), the reviewer sees it as a delete in the plan output before anything actually happens.
items.reference:
📋 Plan shows — "3 to create, 1 to update, 0 to delete"
👀 Human reviews — catches a mistake before it's real

Why: a plan's value is entirely in being reviewable before commitment — applying blind defeats the point of computing it at all.

items.prompt: L2's drift diagram compares the state file's record against the actual cloud. What triggers a drift finding?
choices: The state file's record for a resource no longer matches what's actually running in the cloud
The declared configuration file has a syntax error
The IaC tool hasn't been run in over a week
Two different engineers have access to the same cloud account
items.explanation: Drift is specifically a mismatch between what the state file records (what the tool believes is true) and what's actually running — not a config error or an access issue.
items.reference:
📄 State file — the tool's memory
☁️ Actual cloud — what's really running
⚠️ Drift — comparison finds a mismatch

Why: drift detection is fundamentally a comparison — without a remembered prior state, there's nothing to compare current reality against.

items.prompt: If a team used IaC but never ran drift detection, would the console change from the opening scenario have been caught automatically?
choices: No — drift detection is a deliberate comparison step; without running it, the tool has no reason to notice the state file and reality have diverged
Yes — IaC tools automatically detect every change the instant it happens
Yes, but only for database resources, never for servers
No — IaC tools are incapable of ever detecting drift under any circumstances
items.explanation: Drift detection requires actually running the comparison — having a state file makes drift detectable, but the tool still has to be told to check, the same way plan has to be run to see what would change.
items.reference:

☁️ Actual cloud — what's really running
⚠️ Drift — comparison finds a mismatch

items.prompt: A team writes a bash script of `aws ec2 modify-instance` commands and checks it into version control. L2 says this still isn't quite "Infrastructure as Code" in the full sense. Why?
choices: Being version-controlled isn't the same as being declarative — the script still can't detect drift or guarantee idempotency on its own
Bash scripts can never be checked into version control
Only Python scripts count as real Infrastructure as Code
The script would fail to run on any cloud provider
items.explanation: Version control gives history and review, but it doesn't give the script a state file to diff against — without that, it still can't detect drift or safely guarantee that re-running it is a no-op.
items.reference:
📁 Version-controlled script — has history, still imperative
❌ Missing — no state file, no diff, no drift detection

Why: "checked into git" and "declarative" are independent properties — a script can have one without the other.

items.prompt: What specific capability does a script of cloud CLI commands lack, even if it's well-organized and version-controlled, compared to a true declarative IaC tool?
choices: A state file to diff against, which is what enables both idempotency guarantees and drift detection
The ability to run more than once
The ability to be read by more than one engineer
The ability to be stored in a file at all
items.explanation: The defining capability a declarative tool has that a script lacks is the state file — the record that makes both "is this safe to re-run" and "has anything drifted" answerable questions.
items.reference:
📁 Version-controlled script — has history, still imperative
❌ Missing — no state file, no diff, no drift detection

Why: "checked into git" and "declarative" are independent properties — a script can have one without the other.

items.prompt: L2's failure modes list warns against manually editing infrastructure "just this once" during an incident. Is the manual edit itself the mistake?
choices: No — the manual edit can be a reasonable short-term fix; the mistake is not reconciling the declared config afterward, which turns it into invisible drift
Yes — manual edits should never happen under any circumstances, even during an active incident
No — manual edits are always safe as long as they're documented in a chat message
Yes — the on-call engineer should have waited for the IaC pipeline to run instead of fixing the incident
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that the fix itself was real and necessary — the failure is not following up to update the declared configuration, which is what turns a reasonable emergency action into silent, undetected drift.
items.reference:
🔥 During incident — manual fix is reasonable
⚠️ Afterward — must update declared config, or it becomes drift

Why: this is the opening scenario's exact failure mode — the manual action wasn't wrong, the follow-up was missing.

items.prompt: What turns a reasonable, necessary manual infrastructure change during an incident into a future outage risk?
choices: Not updating the declared configuration afterward, so the change exists only in the actual infrastructure and nowhere the team's process can see it
The fact that the change happened during business hours instead of at night
The specific cloud provider being used
The size of the resource that was changed
items.explanation: The change itself solved a real problem — what makes it dangerous is that it never became visible anywhere else, so any later process (like a routine deploy) has no way to know about it and can silently undo it.
items.reference:
🔥 During incident — manual fix is reasonable
⚠️ Afterward — must update declared config, or it becomes drift

Why: this is the opening scenario's exact failure mode — the manual action wasn't wrong, the follow-up was missing.

items.prompt: L2 explains that idempotency is what a diff-based plan "naturally gives you." What does an imperative script need instead to achieve the same safety?
choices: Deliberate, careful checks at every single step, since safety isn't automatic the way it is with a diff-based plan
Nothing — imperative scripts are always just as safe to re-run as declarative tools
A faster network connection to the cloud provider
Running the script only once per calendar year
items.explanation: A declarative tool's plan step naturally computes only what's actually different; an imperative script has no such built-in check, so achieving the same safety requires the script's author to add explicit "is this already true" checks at every step by hand.
items.reference:
📋 Declarative — safety comes free from diffing
📜 Imperative — safety requires manual, careful checks everywhere

Why: this is the practical cost of choosing imperative scripts over declarative tools — the safety property has to be engineered by hand instead of coming from the approach itself.

items.prompt: Why does a diff-based plan naturally support safe re-application after a failure, without extra work from the tool's author?
choices: Because computing "what's actually different" is already the core mechanism — a second run against the same desired state simply finds fewer or no differences
Because the tool automatically retries failed operations up to three times
Because diff-based plans are always faster than imperative scripts
Because the cloud provider guarantees idempotency on its own
items.explanation: The diff mechanism itself is what makes re-running safe: since the plan step always computes the actual difference between desired and current state, a second run naturally finds less (or nothing) left to do — this isn't a separate feature bolted on, it's inherent to how the diff works.
items.reference:
📋 Declarative — safety comes free from diffing
📜 Imperative — safety requires manual, careful checks everywhere

Why: this is the practical cost of choosing imperative scripts over declarative tools — the safety property has to be engineered by hand instead of coming from the approach itself.

items.prompt: Implement `diffResources(desired, current)`. Both arguments are arrays of `{ id, type, config }` objects. Return `{ toCreate, toUpdate, toDelete }`: `toCreate` holds resources in `desired` but not `current` (by id); `toUpdate` holds resources present in both whose `config` differs (compare with `JSON.stringify`); `toDelete` holds resources in `current` but not `desired`.

tests.expr: (() => { const desired = [{ id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }]; const r = diffResources(desired, []); expect(r.toCreate.length).toBe(1); return expect(r.toCreate[0].id).toBe('a'); })()

tests.description: identical config on both sides produces no changes
tests.expr: (() => { const res = { id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }; const r = diffResources([res], [res]); expect(r.toCreate.length).toBe(0); expect(r.toUpdate.length).toBe(0); return expect(r.toDelete.length).toBe(0); })()

tests.description: a config change on an existing id goes to toUpdate, not toCreate or toDelete
tests.expr: (() => { const current = [{ id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }]; const desired = [{ id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'large' } }]; const r = diffResources(desired, current); expect(r.toUpdate.length).toBe(1); expect(r.toCreate.length).toBe(0); return expect(r.toDelete.length).toBe(0); })()

tests.description: a resource missing from desired goes to toDelete
tests.expr: (() => { const current = [{ id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }, { id: 'b', type: 'database', config: { size: 'medium' } }]; const desired = [{ id: 'b', type: 'database', config: { size: 'medium' } }]; const r = diffResources(desired, current); expect(r.toDelete.length).toBe(1); return expect(r.toDelete[0].id).toBe('a'); })()

items.explanation: Building lookup maps by id lets the function classify each resource in one pass: present only in desired means create, present in both with different config means update, present only in current means delete. This is exactly L3's diffResources, node-verified for idempotency (identical config produces zero changes) and for correctly distinguishing an update from a create+delete pair.
items.reference:
➕ toCreate — in desired, not in current
✏️ toUpdate — in both, config differs
➖ toDelete — in current, not in desired

Why: this is L3's exact diffResources — the same function that later feeds applyPlan and gets reused conceptually for drift detection.

items.prompt: Implement `detectDrift(stateFile, actualCloud)`. `stateFile` is an array of `{ id, type, config }` objects (what the tool last applied). `actualCloud` is a `Map` keyed by id holding what's actually running. Return an array of `{ id, reason }` objects: `reason: "deleted outside IaC"` if a stateFile resource is missing from actualCloud, `reason: "config changed outside IaC"` if it exists but its `config` differs (compare with `JSON.stringify`). Resources that match exactly should not appear in the result.

tests.description: returns an empty array when everything matches
tests.expr: (() => { const stateFile = [{ id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }]; const actual = new Map([['a', { id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }]]); return expect(detectDrift(stateFile, actual).length).toBe(0); })()

tests.description: detects a config change as drift with the correct reason
tests.expr: (() => { const stateFile = [{ id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }]; const actual = new Map([['a', { id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'xlarge' } }]]); const r = detectDrift(stateFile, actual); expect(r.length).toBe(1); expect(r[0].id).toBe('a'); return expect(r[0].reason).toBe('config changed outside IaC'); })()

tests.description: detects a deleted resource as drift with the correct reason
tests.expr: (() => { const stateFile = [{ id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }]; const actual = new Map(); const r = detectDrift(stateFile, actual); expect(r.length).toBe(1); return expect(r[0].reason).toBe('deleted outside IaC'); })()

tests.description: only reports the resources that actually drifted, not ones that match
tests.expr: (() => { const stateFile = [{ id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }, { id: 'b', type: 'database', config: { size: 'medium' } }]; const actual = new Map([['a', { id: 'a', type: 'server', config: { size: 'small' } }], ['b', { id: 'b', type: 'database', config: { size: 'large' } }]]); const r = detectDrift(stateFile, actual); expect(r.length).toBe(1); return expect(r[0].id).toBe('b'); })()

items.explanation: For each resource the tool believes it applied, checking whether it still exists in actualCloud (and with matching config) reveals exactly what changed outside the tool's knowledge. This is L3's exact detectDrift, node-verified against both a config-change case and a deletion case, reproducing the opening scenario's console-resize drift precisely.
items.reference:
📄 stateFile — what the tool believes is true
☁️ actualCloud — what's really running
⚠️ Mismatch — reported with a specific reason

Why: this is L3's exact detectDrift — the function that catches the opening scenario's console resize after the fact.

items.prompt: L3 node-verifies the opening scenario's drift mechanism directly. What specifically does `detectDrift(stateFile1, actualCloudWithDrift)` return in that verification?
choices: A single drift entry for web-1 with reason "config changed outside IaC"
